title: Take On Mars
text: Take on Mars is more simulation than game, and clearly showing that the goal was a simulation first, and a game second. That said, it remains very interesting and works quite well as a game, when you can figure out how to do things and get it to work. And that is one of the problems. The biggest problem however is the complete lack of time acceleration and slow speeds. I understand wanting realistic speeds in your simulation game, but this is not an experience that any but the most patient people are willing to go through. For reference, to complete the unmanned campaign you will need to travel ~50,000m at speeds between 1.5m/s and 2m/s, or in more understandable terms, your rovers go at the speed of an old man with a walking aid and you need to travel roughly a small country's length. The game does helpfully offer you a realistic wheel speeds option, which will bring your speed down to around 0.6m/s, or roughly the speed of that old man if he had to stop to take a breather after every step. I firmly believe that I am one of the most patient people in the world and submit this game as proof for that. With the biggest problem out of the way, the smaller problems are still noticable. It essentially does not tell you how to do or use most things. When starting a campaign, the first thing I had to do was push every button on my keyboard in the hopes that it would move along the interactive first landing of an historical Russian lander. It worked eventually, and I could play the game after that. After that, you are never told how to use specific instruments, and you aren't told what technologies actually do for you as a player. But that is something you can figure out as well with a lot of looking for things, so eventually it will work out. There also still appear to be a fair amount of bugs in the game, including random missions asking you to take microscope pictures of the atmosphere, and one that makes it so missions do not spawn when they should so the game literally becomes unfinishable. With the last one in mind, I had to stop my playthrough before I could get to the manned stage, as the missions I needed to complete did not ever show up. The physics at times become a large problem in that your science instruments need to be held still to do science, but the physics tries to make your rovers almost dance, which makes it nearly impossible to use your instruments unless you forcibly jam them against the rock or sand you are trying to perform experiments on. Even then, Mars is a nice and often varied place, with a lot of interesting terrain and good looking locations, with missions placed so that they show you to all the good places with almost scenic tours. The economic part of the game- Getting your funding, is very rough early on and practically doesn't exist in the later stages. This may be to save up money for the manned missions, but I never actually reached that part, so I wouldn't know. All things said, Take on Mars needs work. It is not an unpleasant experience for one with a lot of patience, but I struggle to see what would draw in anyone other than the most scientific minded people who at the same time don't mind gameplay. For anyone else, it is a nice novelty, but very repetitive and slow. There does not seem to be that much here, at least not in the unmanned campaign. There is also a multiplayer mode, but I've yet to be able to motivate anyone into playing it with me. I will update this review whenever I get people into a server with it.

title: Take On Mars
text: While the basic idea of this game is terrific, the execution is lacking in major ways. I really hope the developers continue to shape the main aspects of this game, as the concept does have a lot of potential. The big issue in my point of view, and why I'd not recommend it at this time: Very linear gameplay, for an exploration game it lacks the "open world" feeling. This is immediately evident when you execute your first mission, you can see a rectangular plane of mars, your mission area, floating in the void of space, in the early descent phase. The career part is mission based, so instead of conducting free-form exploration, the player launches a vehicle to perform a very specific set of tasks. The first ten missions you will launch for example consist of nothing more than selecting a point on the map, launch the vehicle, look at the descent phase, wait for the "exploration accomplished" info to pop up, and immediately disconnect from the vehicle as the mission is done even before you touch down. The next couple of missions involve you actually waiting until touchdown, activate one instrument, and disconnect. The vehicle design suffers from similar issues, it is just way too linear. You basically select a chassis, stick some instruments in predefined slots, without any real freedom in design. I really want to like this game, and in fact I do not regret investing the 15 bucks as it might get somewhere someday, but at this time there simply does not come up any real fun playing this.

title: Take On Mars
text: --For those wanting to just get to a hands on review skip to the secondary section.-- I have been watching and following, and in the past had time to help with hunting bugs and harassing the devs with copy pasted reports since it first came out on early access. Over time I have gotten to see this game grow more and more, thus expanding it's own potential. Take On Mars not only is a simulator, but an educational platform (Hence the wiki data you unlock in the Robotics portion.). With games like this, and Kerbal Space Program, I see a lot of potential for games to bring new challenges and focus to many forms of education in simulation that can even be utilized in classrooms to get kids interested in space exploration, physics, astrobiology, and aeronautics through adaptive and hands on learning. I know it's been a long time, and yes the due date has been pushed back, and yes there are still bugs that need to be smashed. But in the end, Take On Mars will be a perfect platform for both simulation lovers, and Mars Enthusiasts as the work put into this makes it one of the most unique games currently in beta. Long strides have been made in gaming technology that opens up more intuitive and complex forms of learning and adapting to in game demands through user comprehension and skill. This game needs as much notice and support as possible. ------------------------------------------------Section Two-------------------------------------- Take On Mars is a game based on the research of Mars in understanding what is to be expected for human crews to work with. In the first portion you are able to utilize probes, lander, rovers, and advanced equipment to study the martian surface and gather real world intel based on scientific findings. In chapter two you will take the role of a surviving astronaut who has to survive on the surface through building and maintaining equipment (Chapter2 is still in development.) Also there are singleplayer and multiplayer scenarios, along with an editor so that you can build your own scenario and upload it to the workshop. Along with this is the ability to easily mod the game files via the developer toolset if you're into that. This gives grounds so a lot of malleability to the game and what players can do with it. Overall, despite it being unfinished I have to give it a 8/10 for both the improvements, the dev team, and the uniqueness of the game. There are others sure, like Mars: Challenger, which is fun but not one I can honestly recommend. All in all, Take On Mars is a gem, and to those wondering if it is worth buying I will say this: If you don't mind putting in the effort to submit bug reports, push the game mechanics, and test different aspects of the game then yes, buy it and help the developers expand and debug more of it. If you want something polished off the bat and are not patient or willing to aid in development, then no, and nor should you buy any game on Early Access because that is what it is for.

title: Tales of Berseria™
text: A Quick Review For A Rather Persistently Insistent Mate Of Mine ;p Comparison Comment: Those of you who've got into any of the Tales Of games (Zestiria, Symphonia) will feel right at home here; next to no changes I've seen so far. At A Glance: Given that I've heard some folks out there taking 60-80 hours to complete their first attempt, I'm barely into the game here so can't cover much ;) So far I've had my Happy-Go-Lucky Dragonball Level Martial Arts Student enjoying a blissful life in The Innocent Village In The Land Of Milk And Honey which suddenly has ***An Event*** which is almost on par with The Eclipse from Berserk, which leads to Wrongful Imprisonment and am now coming up to the part where the MC is going on a Roaring Rampage Of Revenge... So yep; pretty standard fare so far :D What got me is just how QUICK the game went from Happyland to Grimdark; normally there's a bit of build-up before you get thrown into the deep end (literally, in this case), so that made for a good change of pace. Combat is in real-time and not turn-based, but there are cool-downs for your abilities which you have to keep check of when you're in the thick of it. It doesn't take your mind off the action, but something to be mindful of - you generally blitzkrieg through the combats once you get to a certain point anyway - might become more of a priority when you're doing Boss Runs I'm thinking. Story is... okay, it's pretty cliche' so far, but don't let that put you off; it's well-delivered in my opinion and doesn't feel re-hashed/a carbon copy of other games. I've yet to get the full details on The Grand Conspiracy but I'm very much looking forward to when I can put down The Big Bad with extreme prejudice :D The MC (Velvet) is basically a girl cloned from Guts' genes, which I appreciate in my MCs ;D character development seems to be pretty detailed, so I find it a bit of a pity that you can't have 'interactive paths' which would have added to the experience. But it's not that kind of RPG, so I'll live with it :) Not going to go too much further in as I've dropped enough light spoilers as it is, but let's give you a score out of ten from me: 9.75/10 .25 is coming off from slightly fiddly menu controls ;p So to my Persistently Insistent Mate - just hurry up and bloody well buy the game already!!!

text: A very good PC port and it changes up the series in good ways, most accessible combat in years.  This would be a great Tales game to start with. Tales of is basically the same game for 20 years with slooow changes and the same overall plot in different clothes - whenever they mess with that, like Legendia, the fans get upset. They've changed up the plot a bit to make it a little less formula, but can't really say how without spoilers. I like it though. The other key thing is that the combat is as hard as you want it to be.  Zesteria was getting ridiculously obtuse and I couldn't recommend it to anyone new.  With Berseria you can literally hammer the A button and trigger breaks with the RT and win .  On the other hand, you can go as deep as you want, so once you get bored with hammering A the deeper combat is still there. Dub voicework is pretty decent, English Magilou is fantastic. I'm playing with Japanese audio now just for Velvet, but you can totally do English without cringing.

title: Tales of Berseria™
text: My last game from Tales Series on PC, this one was truly  wonderful. It improves on Zesteria in almost every way, and while its story didn't have the same massive impact as Symphonia did,  the great characters, in my opinion, make up for it. What you end up with is a Tales game with a great story, great characters, and the best gameplay so far. The game is easy to get into, as the equipment system is streamlined from Zesteria's overly compliacted skill system, with enhancement being a linear process with the materials required being somewhat difficult to come by. It's also quite obvious which items are safe to sell, most of the time - being equipment you have copies of or "miscellaneous" items you can mostly find by picking up everywhere. The combat is a little more complicated, in that souls limit the length of your combos, and your combos are almost completely customisable, provided your controlling a character manually. This is mostly good, though it can be difficult ot figure out which moves flow together well, and to construct a moveset that'll cover most enemy types and weaknesses. However, the AI is so good that sometimes it's better to let them handle controlling your character. You also rarely need to worry about taking care of your other members in combat because of this. The story is refreshing darker than the last games, as the protagnist is for once not a bright, cheerful and optimistic hero. More of an anti-hero, Velvet and her party's adventures are different and kept me guessing on how their journey would go. The outfit though... was a bit too striperific, know what I mean? Oh well. The chracters were great, and the dialogue this time was well written... though the subtitles had quite a few errors, which may have been due to localisation errors. Still I loved the skits more than ever between the characters, and was mostly sucked into the story due to these great characters, not so much the story itself. Lastly, the graphics were great, soliid 60 FPS throughout the game, and the environments look gorgeous. The only real negative of the game is how each environment doesn't change much as you go through, making it somewhat boring to navigate dungeons and fields. Music is OK, though it really shines during the emotional moments. Probably one of the best JRPGs I've ever played, I'd recommend this to any RPG fan, or anime fan that like games too. I will miss this game, and its characters, in a similar way I loved Symphonia, and other great RPGs like Baldur's  Gate 2. A truly wonderful game.

title: Tap Tap Infinity
text: Another great Clicker game, this one is very simlar to Clicker Heroes (CH), HOWEVER, it does have some twists and a very unique ability to stand its own ground! 1) A Story (ok, not really much) 2) Better IDLE mode (you contimue to conquer levels, in addition to money) 3) RANKs... they are the true mechanics, after the skills which are almost 1:1 from CH. You gain Ranks by beating waves of monsters.... and after 500 (and then 600...), you can decide to wipe your Rank grogress to advance to the next Rank level, which gives now a higher DPS boost per level! 4) Most innovative Skill: BossRush! You skill the normal waves and jist do Boss waves for a limited amount of time, and can therefore skip a huge amount of levels to again reach those levels where you now might be stron enough... makes full runbs much faster and less grindy, great invention! 5) Gem based DPS boost... several ways to choose which hero should get boosted by VERY limited resource (either DPS or helper skills (+xxx Gold...) 6) Mystery gift... every 30min, you get a short window where you can click 1 of 3 gifts... can be Gold, Valorpoints, Infinity Tokens or (very rarely) Gems + Nice achievements make it worthwhile to continue and get stronger. Therefore, 9/10. Would have been perfect without the Gems, which are too rare, and which are too much of a cash grab (can be bough for real money)

title: Tap Tap Infinity
text: This game was recommended to me by a friend who loves clickers, and I like clickers, too. Clickers are a type of "time management" game, a la Facebook games, where it behooves you to micromanage, but after a few, it's best to leave and come back the next day in real life. I played Tap Tap Infinity to detox from the addictive Clicker Heroes, the game responsible for the theme of the Steam Monster Sale. Tap Tap Infinity is a lot like Clicker Heroes, as in, the game has a lot of complexity for a clicker and has many of the same Gods - expect to prestige a lot, and the clicking "spells" to cast are ususble throughout the entire game.  There is a calculator on the internet to advise on what the best way to prestige is - either through more gold or more damage, and the game soft restarts with these bonuses permanently.  There are ways of exporting your save file, but it is still possible to lose this if your computer breaks - try to keep a save file on Pastebin or something as a backup, as with Clicker Heroes.  If you do, or if you're frustrated with the game, you can always copy/paste a completed save file and grab all the achievements, if you need to detox from all this addictiveness, or get plain frustrated. This game is not a cash grab, although there are premium gods which will increase your pace a few fold, but these gods are like 1 dollar each American to get, and there's no real reason to put more than 10 dollars in this game.  The worst clickers make it so it's several times harder to progress every 10 levels, making it so you must keep putting money into the game or bust - this is not one of those. I've played on and off for 2 years, and I've finally beaten the game. Finished, polished, has an ending to the game - 5 stars.

Pretty generic, but the graphics and characters are nice and cartoony with fun humerous names and abilities, OH and after hiring a boss to fight for you you level and give them abilities that help your clicker or your dps with the gold you get for killing thus baddies and monsters. There are infinity tokens you get for restarting the game and beating up too so many level(s) bosses that help you get better and better with dps or clicker or gold income upgrades. Nice, but you have to restart. They're given to you by 4 infinity gods that'll give you the tokens and want you to find out why baddies are baddies that wern't always baddies.
